meta.theme: whether language shapes thought: obligatory grammatical marking as a habit of attention built by repetition, replacing the picture of a grammar that walls off what its speakers can think

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS; no external source adapted. Personal study only.

meta.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
meta.reviewer_notes: A foundation-level passage on a topic usually written badly. The familiar strong claim is stated and refused in the second paragraph, so every question is really a test of whether the reader kept the refusal. No named languages and no trivia: the illustration is hypothetical on purpose.

quality.adversarial_review: Three accounts of the findings now run through the set. The shadow is the softened wall: the grammar does limit thought, only mildly, so an unmarked distinction is harder to hold in mind and the habit is how the limit operates. It carries an option in every question (Q1 'more effort to hold in mind', Q3 the title about thoughts made harder, Q4 'retained in the weaker form it can support') and it dies on the flattest sentences in the passage — 'Nothing is missing from their minds' and speakers who 'draw it as competently as anyone else', which leave no residue of difficulty to be weakened into. The second rival reverses the arrow: a community comes to care about a distinction and its grammar later marks it. The passage never discusses where an obligation came from, and its mechanism runs the other way, from a requirement met thousands of times a day to a settled habit. The third rival takes the second paragraph's concession for the conclusion and denies any cognitive difference at all, treating the findings as artefacts of the speaking task; the fourth paragraph says the difference should shrink in non-linguistic tasks, not vanish, and 'That is roughly what is observed' is offered as a confirmation of a real difference rather than as its dissolution. Q2 has been rebuilt: it previously handed a blind reader three statements of the moderate position and named the rejected one as its answer, which announced the passage's whole shape. The three true options are now local facts about the text, and the false one is a precise misstatement of the condition under which an obligatory category is settled — 'not because the matter is important on that occasion, but because there is no grammatical way round it'. Strength parity was imposed across the set afterwards: no distractor in this file is quantified more strongly than its key, because a single overreaching option was found to condemn the whole reading it belonged to without the passage being read.

blind_solve.notes: full agreement Options rebuilt against an explicit shadow thesis (a coherent rival reading carried across every question in the passage) so that the option sets no longer form a single consistent clique; the item awaits a re-solve. A second pass then removed the strength asymmetry two blind readers named as the residual channel: every distractor is now hedged no more strongly than its key, and where the passage itself asserts something flatly the key carries the absolute, so that the most cautious option is no longer reliably the answer. A third pass closed four key-to-key paraphrase and entailment leaks between questions, replaced the true options of the NOT item with framing rather than mechanism, and removed two distractors that hardening had made true. A fourth pass repaired two distractors that hardening had made defensible (an inference option entailed on a causal reading, and a purpose option with no false half) and removed a shape cue from the NOT item.

paragraphs.text: The question of whether language shapes thought usually arrives in a form that cannot be answered. Does a language allow its speakers thoughts that another language forbids? Put that way the answer is almost certainly no. People translate, borrow, explain and invent, and no idea has yet been found that stops at a border. But there is a smaller question underneath the large one, and the smaller question does have an answer. Speakers of different languages, asked to sort pictures or to describe a scene from memory, sometimes attend to different features of the same event, consistently, and without any sense of doing anything unusual.

The familiar explanation is that a language builds walls: what your grammar has no room for, you cannot easily think. It is a congenial picture and it does not fit the findings. Speakers whose language leaves a distinction unmarked can be shown it, taught it, and asked about it, and they draw it as competently as anyone else. Nothing is missing from their minds. Something is different about their habits.

The difference lies in what a grammar obliges. Every language lets its speakers say anything; only some make them say particular things every time. Imagine a language in which you cannot report that a vase broke without also indicating whether you saw it break or were told about it. A speaker of that language has to settle the question of evidence before the sentence will close — not because the matter is important on that occasion, but because there is no grammatical way round it. Do that a few thousand times a day for a lifetime, and how you know a thing becomes something you have already worked out before anyone asks.

This accounts for the findings without the walls. What differs between speakers is not what can be thought but what is routinely attended to, and habits of attention are made by repetition rather than by limitation. The explanation also makes a prediction the wall picture does not: the difference between speakers should be largest when they are preparing to speak, and should shrink when the task has nothing to do with language at all. That is roughly what is observed. A language does not decide what its speakers may think. It decides what they must have thought about by the time they reach the end of a sentence.

questions.target_mistake: treating a difference in attention as a difference in capacity, reversing the arrow between grammar and habit, or concluding from the second paragraph that no difference survives outside speech
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: the passage separates what speakers notice from what speakers can understand, so any safe inference will keep the two apart.
questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Two speakers may differ in what they notice about an event without differing at all in what they can understand about it.
options.B: A distinction its language leaves unmarked takes its speakers more effort to hold in mind.
options.C: A community first comes to care about a distinction, and its grammar later develops an obligatory way of marking it.
options.D: The differences observed between speakers appear only while they are preparing to speak.

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph does two things in four sentences: it denies a difference in capacity, in the flattest words available — 'Nothing is missing from their minds' — and asserts a difference in habit. An inference question on this passage is decided by whether an option keeps both halves at the strength the passage gives them.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option holds those two findings side by side, and takes the second at the passage's own strength. The difference in noticing is real; the difference in capacity is not merely small but absent, since anyone can be shown the distinction and will then draw it as competently as anyone else. So an option that says the speakers do not differ at all in what they can understand is reporting the passage rather than overshooting it, and the flat word is the author's.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question rewards the option the sentences force, which is sometimes the unhedged one: where a passage denies something outright, the safe inference denies it outright too.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says a difference is real but not a limitation, write both halves down, and write down how strongly each is put. Options will offer you the difference with the limitation smuggled back in, the limitation with the difference removed, or the right claim at the wrong strength.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage leaves no difficulty to be softened. Speakers whose language leaves a distinction unmarked 'can be shown it, taught it, and asked about it, and they draw it as competently as anyone else', and the paragraph ends 'Nothing is missing from their minds.' A wall reduced to a slope is still a wall, and the passage says there is no wall.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the reasonable-sounding middle between the picture the passage rejects and the one it offers, and it is hedged exactly as a careful claim would be.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage runs the arrow from grammar to attention: obligation forces a settlement thousands of times a day and a habit follows. It says nothing at all about how a language came to have the obligation in the first place.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like the sensible, non-mystical account of where such grammar comes from, and the passage's dislike of strong claims makes a modest-sounding one feel welcome.

distractors.why_wrong: The prediction is that the difference 'should be largest when they are preparing to speak, and should shrink when the task has nothing to do with language at all'. Shrinking is not disappearing, and the passage offers the pattern as confirmation that a habit of attention is real rather than as a sign that it exists only on the way to a sentence.
distractors.seductive_element: It is built from the passage's own prediction and takes the half of it a reader remembers, since the striking claim is that the difference is largest in speech and the qualifying half is a single subordinate clause.

questions.target_mistake: rejecting one of the passage's own framing claims because it is paraphrased, and so missing the one statement that contradicts the answer the opening paragraph gives to the large question
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true, according to the passage?

options.A: People translate, borrow and invent, and no idea has yet been found that stops at a border.
options.B: Speakers who attend to different features do so inconsistently, from one occasion to the next.
options.C: Speakers of different languages sometimes attend to different features of the same event.
options.D: Speakers who attend differently have no sense that they are doing anything unusual.

explanation.expert_notice: The first paragraph states the finding with three qualifications packed into one clause: speakers 'sometimes attend to different features of the same event, consistently, and without any sense of doing anything unusual'. Each of those words is doing work, and consistently is the one the rest of the passage depends on.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option denies the word the argument needs. A difference that came and went from one occasion to the next would be noise, and nothing in the passage would follow: the explanation offered is a settled habit built by an obligation met thousands of times a day, and a habit of that kind is precisely what shows up consistently. The passage says so in the same breath in which it reports the finding, which is why the other three options, each a plain report of something the opening paragraph asserts, are all true.
explanation.question_type_note: In a NOT-true question the three true statements are often the passage's framing rather than its argument, so hunting for the main claim is the wrong procedure; test each option against the sentence it came from, and watch the adverbs.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage reports a finding, read its adverbs as claims rather than as decoration. Sometimes, consistently and without any sense of it are three separate assertions, and a detail question will usually take back exactly one of them.

distractors.why_wrong: The first paragraph says it directly — 'People translate, borrow, explain and invent, and no idea has yet been found that stops at a border' — and this option keeps the same hedge, yet, rather than claiming that no such idea could exist.
distractors.seductive_element: The sweep of the sentence makes it look like the kind of overstatement a careful passage would avoid, which invites a reader to mark it false on style.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the finding the whole passage exists to explain, stated in the first paragraph: speakers 'sometimes attend to different features of the same event, consistently'. The hedge is the passage's own.
distractors.seductive_element: It is so modest a claim that a reader looking for the passage's argument may take it for a watered-down version of something stronger the passage said.

distractors.why_wrong: The same sentence supplies it: the differences appear 'without any sense of doing anything unusual'. It is a detail about how the finding presents itself, and the passage states it as part of the finding.
distractors.seductive_element: It is a claim about what speakers are aware of, which sounds like the sort of thing a passage would have to establish rather than assert.

questions.target_mistake: titling the passage with a softened version of the picture it rejects, with the cultural story it never tells, or with the sceptical conclusion it stops short of
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say before the options: the title must be about obligation, about what a grammar makes a speaker settle, and not about what a grammar forbids.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.A: The Thoughts a Grammar Makes Harder
options.B: Why Cultures Get the Grammar They Need
options.C: What a Language Obliges You to Notice
options.D: A Difference That Vanishes Off the Page

explanation.expert_notice: The last sentence of the passage is written as a title would be: 'A language does not decide what its speakers may think. It decides what they must have thought about by the time they reach the end of a sentence.' A title question on a passage that ends in a formulation is usually decided there.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct title names the mechanism the passage argues for and the effect it produces. Obliges is the passage's own verb for what a grammar does, and notice is what the whole argument is about: routine attention built by repeated requirement. It also covers all four paragraphs, since the finding, the rejected explanation and the accepted one are all about noticing rather than about capacity.
explanation.question_type_note: A title has to be the argument in a few words, which means it must survive the paragraph where the author refuses something. Titles that name a mechanism the passage rejects, or a claim it stops short of, fail that test however well they fit the middle.
explanation.reading_habit: Write your own six-word title before you look at the options, then test each option against the passage's last sentence rather than its most memorable image. A title that would have to be softened or strengthened to fit that sentence is describing a different argument.

distractors.why_wrong: No thought is made harder in this passage. Speakers who lack a marking 'draw it as competently as anyone else' and 'Nothing is missing from their minds'; what differs is what gets settled routinely, not what costs effort. A title that keeps the wall and lowers it names the account the passage refuses.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like the cautious version of a famous claim, and a passage that says the strong version is wrong is expected to keep a mild one.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage runs the arrow from grammar to habit: obligation forces a settlement thousands of times a day and a habit of attention follows. Where an obligatory category came from in the first place is a question the passage never raises, so a title about grammars being acquired to suit a culture's needs names an argument that is not here.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the sensible, non-mystical story a reader supplies unprompted, and the passage's dislike of strong claims makes a modest-sounding title feel welcome.

distractors.why_wrong: The prediction is that the difference should be largest in preparing to speak and 'should shrink when the task has nothing to do with language at all'. Shrinking is offered as confirmation of a habit that is real, and the passage's closing sentence says what a language does decide, which a title announcing a vanishing difference denies.
distractors.seductive_element: It picks up the passage's genuine deflation of the large question and reads as the sceptical verdict a corrective piece is expected to reach.

questions.target_mistake: describing the passage as a claim weakened into survival, or as a cultural explanation, when the second paragraph refuses one account outright and the fourth puts its replacement to a test
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to sketch the skeleton before the options: a puzzling finding, a popular explanation refused, a narrower explanation offered, and a prediction used to test it.
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the structure of the passage?

options.A: A strong claim is stated, weakened by evidence, and retained in the weaker form it can support.
options.B: A finding is reported, the usual explanation of it is refused, and a narrower one is offered and tested.
options.C: A familiar question is set aside, a finding is reported, and its cause is traced to the community.
options.D: A finding is reported and then shown to be an artefact of the way it was measured.

explanation.expert_notice: Each paragraph announces its job. The first ends with a finding about what speakers attend to; the second says the familiar explanation 'does not fit the findings'; the third gives the alternative; the fourth derives a prediction and reports that it holds. That is four moves, in that order.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names those four moves in the order the passage makes them. It also captures the relation between the two explanations, which is not a comparison but a replacement: the wall account is refused on evidence, and the obligation account is then required to earn its place by predicting something the refused account does not.
explanation.question_type_note: Structure questions ask about the skeleton, not the subject. Label each paragraph with a verb as you read, and then choose the option whose verbs match yours in the same order.
explanation.reading_habit: Sketch the argument in four words before you read the options: finding, refusal, alternative, test. An option that changes even one of those verbs is describing a different passage.

distractors.why_wrong: The wall account is not weakened and kept; it is refused and replaced. 'Nothing is missing from their minds. Something is different about their habits' discards one explanation and announces another, and the fourth paragraph then asks the new one to earn its place by predicting something the old one does not.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does open by cutting a large question down to a small one, so a reader who takes that opening move for the whole shape will expect a claim surviving in reduced form.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage does set the large question aside and does report a finding, and then it traces the finding to an obligation in the grammar and the repetition that obligation enforces. The community that might have shaped the grammar is never mentioned, so the third move names a cause the passage does not supply.
distractors.seductive_element: Its first two clauses describe the opening paragraph exactly, and an option that begins correctly is rarely read to the end.

distractors.why_wrong: The finding is reported and then explained, not dissolved. The prediction about non-linguistic tasks is offered as a test the explanation passes, and the passage's last sentence states positively what a language decides, which a passage that had explained its finding away would have nothing to say.
distractors.seductive_element: The prediction that the difference shrinks off the page really is in the passage, and a shrinking difference sounds like a finding being taken back.

vocabulary.passage_use: The difference lies in what a grammar obliges.
vocabulary.meaning_here: compels as a condition of speaking at all, leaving the speaker no way round it

vocabulary.passage_use: It is a congenial picture and it does not fit the findings
vocabulary.meaning_here: agreeable to the mind; easy and pleasant to believe

vocabulary.passage_use: not what can be thought but what is routinely attended to
vocabulary.meaning_here: noticed and kept in mind as a matter of course

mentor.challenge: A familiar debate, handled unusually. The passage rejects the version of the claim you have probably met, and then makes a smaller one. Keep track of which version is which.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Speakers of different languages really do notice different things about the same event, but not because their grammar forbids certain thoughts; it is because a grammar that obliges a distinction makes its speakers settle that question thousands of times a day, and repetition turns settlement into a habit of attention.
mentor.main_idea: Language does not limit what people can think. What it can do is force them to settle certain questions every time they speak. Do that often enough and you are in the habit of noticing something that speakers of other languages have no particular reason to notice. The differences researchers find are differences of habit, not of ability.
mentor.simple_explanation:
People often ask whether your language controls your thinking. Asked in the strongest way — can a language stop you having a thought? — the answer seems to be no. People translate, borrow words and explain things, and no idea has been found that gets stuck at a border.

But there is a smaller question that does have an answer. When researchers ask speakers of different languages to sort pictures or describe a remembered scene, the speakers sometimes pay attention to different parts of the same event, over and over, without realising they are doing it.

The popular explanation is that grammar builds walls: if your language has no room for an idea, you cannot really think it. That is a nice picture and it is wrong. Take a speaker whose language does not mark some distinction, show it to them, explain it, ask them about it, and they handle it perfectly well. Nothing is missing from their heads.

What is different is habit, and the cause is obligation. Every language can express anything; only some force you to express particular things every time. Imagine a language where you cannot say 'the vase broke' without also saying whether you saw it happen or were told. Then you have to decide how you know, every single time, whether or not you care. Do that thousands of times a day for years, and the question of how you know is already answered before anyone asks it.

This explains the results without any walls. It also predicts something the wall story does not: the difference between speakers should be biggest when they are about to speak and much smaller when the task has nothing to do with language. That is what researchers find. So a language does not decide what you may think. It decides what you must have thought about by the time your sentence ends.
mentor.why_difficult: The difficulty is not in the vocabulary but in holding two similar-sounding claims apart. The passage states a strong claim, rejects it, and then makes a weaker one that uses many of the same words, so a reader who remembers the topic rather than the argument will carry the rejected version into the questions. The image of walls is the most vivid thing in the piece, and it belongs to the view the author refuses, which is exactly why it appears among the options as a title and as an answer.
mentor.author_intention: To rescue a real finding from an exciting but false explanation, and to leave the reader with a mechanism plain enough to use: obligation, repetition, habit.

paragraph_journey.note: The big version of the question has no answer worth having. The smaller one does: speakers of different languages notice different parts of the same event, consistently.
The idea that grammar walls off thought is attractive and does not match the evidence. Show an unmarked speaker the distinction and they draw it perfectly.
Some grammars force you to settle a matter before a sentence can end. Do that thousands of times a day and you have already decided before you are asked.
Habit, not limitation. The account predicts the effect shrinks in tasks that are not about speaking, which is what is observed, and the passage closes on the distinction it has been defending.

mentor.tone_progression: Level and slightly impatient with the way the question is usually posed, then firmly corrective in the second paragraph, and finally calm and confident, closing on a neat pair of sentences rather than a flourish.
key_transitions: 'But there is a smaller question underneath the large one' (paragraph 1) — the unanswerable question is swapped for an answerable one.
'It is a congenial picture and it does not fit the findings.' (paragraph 2) — the popular explanation is refused.
'The difference lies in what a grammar obliges.' (opening of paragraph 3) — the author's own account begins.
mentor.misunderstanding: Readers in a hurry come away believing the passage says language shapes thought in the usual strong sense, because the walls image is the thing they remember and the passage certainly says that language makes a difference. The actual claim is narrower and more interesting: the difference is in what speakers routinely attend to, built by a requirement they cannot avoid, and it fades when speaking is not involved. Anyone whose summary contains 'cannot think' has summarised the view the author rejects.
mentor.traps_summary: Three moves are punished here. Taking the rejected picture as the thesis, which the title question and the NOT-true question both test. Turning a habit into a universal rule, since a lifelong habit sounds as if it must operate everywhere. And rejecting a true statement because it is paraphrased or stated from the opposite end of a comparison. Check each option against a sentence, not against your memory of the topic.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author states a familiar view before disagreeing with it, mark that view at once and keep it marked. Its vocabulary will come back in the options, because a wrong answer built from the passage's own memorable words is the cheapest trap there is. The test is never whether the words appeared, but whose claim they were serving.
mentor.real_world: Any form that will not let you proceed without answering a question does the same work as such a grammar: filling it in often enough makes you notice something you would otherwise have passed over, which is why the design of forms is quietly powerful.
mentor.takeaway: A language does not limit what you can think; it decides what you cannot leave unsettled.
mentor.reflection_question: What question does your daily routine force you to answer so often that you have stopped noticing you are answering it?
